title: Why the alto took over; no future as a black violinist; Eddie South
summary: Alto was commercial; there were few opportunities for black violinists; Eddie South asked him to join in 1934; he no longer plays violin.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: The alto saxophone rather rapidly became your principal instrument, didn't it?

Well, it became that because it was the most commercial. So, you always have to follow the dollar sign wherever it goes, if you want to survive and survival was always the name of the game. I would have loved to have been a very good violin player, but there was no survival for me as a violin player because there were just no places for a black violin player to be playing. There was only two of them that I'd ever known that were very famous and that was Atwell Rose and Eddie South. Before that -- as a matter of fact, Eddie South wanted me to leave this city here when he came here to work with a place called the Moscow Inn, here on Sunset Strip in 1934. He came out here as a violin player with a

group that had Milt Hinton playing bass in it in 1934 and he wanted me to leave here and play violin and clarinet in his band in 1934, which I wouldn't do because I didn't want to leave Los Angeles. But there was not future for me as a violin player. That's why my uncle gave me the clarinet when I graduated from junior high school and says, "Go out and make some money."
Do you ever play violin now?

Nope. No, I never play violin. I love the instrument too much to play it badly and for me to just pick up a violin now and to play it without playing it well, I would feel as though I was prostituting myself and the instrument and I would never do that. So I won't play under any circumstances, because I would never allow myself to play bad.
